claims.text: The starting coating is a nanoscale multilayer composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The starting multilayer exhibits severe lattice distortion.
The starting multilayer has a low degree of short-range order.
Reducing the FCC/BCC interface spacing enhances mechanically induced short-range-order formation at the interfaces.
Reducing the interface spacing enhances the stability of interfacial short-range order.
Targeted post-deposition thermal treatment promotes short-range-order formation at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Smaller interface spacing increases local interfacial stress fields.
The local stress fields generated by smaller interface spacing promote stable short-range order.
Enhanced interfacial short-range order restricts dislocation glide.
Enhanced interfacial short-range order restricts dislocation climb.
Enhanced interfacial short-range order slows atomic diffusion.
Lower atomic diffusion is associated with greater creep resistance.
Larger interface spacing weakens the proposed constraints on dislocation motion and produces a higher creep rate.
At approximately 1000 K, increasing stress can move creep behavior from diffusion-dominated deformation toward dislocation activity.
Reduced layer thickness combined with thermal treatment will lower atomic diffusion coefficients relative to an untreated intermediate-spacing baseline.
Reduced layer thickness combined with thermal treatment will reduce dislocation activity near interfaces relative to the baseline.
Reduced layer thickness combined with thermal treatment will lower the overall creep rate relative to the baseline.
The proposed effect is significant only within a nanoscale multilayer architecture under high-temperature sustained loading.
The optimum interface-spacing threshold and the interaction between thermal-treatment parameters and dislocation dynamics are not established.
